The search turned up consistent information on running Hurl `.hurl` files in CI. Most of it comes from third-party guides, not hurl.dev, so check the flags against the official docs.

- **Assertions:** Hurl supports implicit asserts on the response line and explicit ones in an `[Asserts]` block. Those run whether or not test mode is on. Test mode only changes output and adds the recap. Common asserts include JSONPath, headers, regex, and response duration.
- **Exit codes:** Test mode is the CI switch. One guide says running with --test treats assertion failures as a non-zero exit code. Another gives a specific code: exit code 4 on assert failure. Without `--test`, the tool acts more like curl and prints the body.
- **Reports:** Flags include `--report-junit` for CI dashboards and `--report-html` for HTML output. One example is `hurl --test --report-junit report.xml tests/*.hurl`.
- **Other useful flags:** `--parallel` runs files concurrently, `--variable` or `--variables-file` set environment values, and `--error-format long` shows the actual response when a check fails.
- **Tooling:** A companion `hurlfmt` binary formats and lints files.

Version details differ by source. One skill page says the current version is 8.0.1, and the exit-code value of 4 appears only in that source, so confirm both on hurl.dev before relying on them.

Bruno's CLI (`@usebruno/cli`) covers most of what you asked about, though the search didn't address offline use directly.

- **Collections and Git:** Bruno keeps collections as plain-text files in a folder on your filesystem, so version control works directly. You can use Git or any version control of your choice to collaborate over your API collections.
- **Running:** From the collection directory, `bru run` runs everything. You can target a single request file or a folder, and select an environment with `--env`. Navigate to the directory where your API collection resides, and then run: bru run. This command will run all the requests in your collection.
- **Assertions:** Results include pass/fail and assertion errors. One guide says built-in Chai-style assertions and JavaScript scripting are supported.
- **CI:** The docs describe CI/CD as a core use. Bruno CLI is designed for CI/CD. Use `--bail` to stop on first failure. Reporters include out-of-the-box JSON, JUnit & HTML outputs for CI dashboards or local debugging. A Docker image is also available for pipelines. Official Docker images for the Bruno CLI let you run API collections in CI/CD pipelines and locally without installing Node.js or npm on the host.
- **Caveats:** Flag syntax differs between sources. The official docs use `--output` for results, while a third-party blog uses `--output junit.xml --format junit` and `--collection`, so check the current reference before copying commands. Two GitHub results are forks, not official sources. Also, variables marked as secrets in the Bruno app aren't exposed via CLI, so they must be passed explicitly.
- **Offline:** Nothing in the results says the CLI works offline. Collections are local files, but requests still go to live endpoints, so an API that isn't reachable will fail. Mocking or a local server would be needed for fully offline runs.

content.text:
**Recommendation: Hurl.** It's free, open source (Apache-2.0), and runs entirely from the command line with no account. Each request is a plain `.hurl` text file with its assertions in the same file, so diffs in code review are easy to read. `hurl --test` returns a non-zero exit code when an assertion fails, which fails the CI job.

**Caveats**
- "Offline" means the tool needs no sign-in or network service. The APIs you test still have to be reachable, so for a fully offline run you'd point the files at a local server or mock.
- Hurl has no GUI. If teammates want a visual client, they'll need a separate app.
- My search results were mostly third-party guides. Check the exit code and flags against the official docs at [hurl.dev](https://hurl.dev) before you rely on them.

**Install (Mac)**
1. Show the command to your team before you run it. Then run `brew install hurl`.
2. Verify with `hurl --version`.

**Install (Linux CI)**
Use the official Linux packages or release tarball from the Hurl install page on hurl.dev. Pin a version so CI doesn't change under you. Avoid piping an install script into a shell.

**First run**
1. Create `tests/users.hurl` in your repo:
   ```
   GET https://api.example.com/users/1

   HTTP 200
   [Asserts]
   jsonpath "$.id" == 1
   ```
2. Run it locally: `hurl --test tests/users.hurl`. A failing assertion prints the actual response and exits non-zero.
3. In CI, run the whole folder and write a JUnit report:
   `hurl --test --report-junit report.xml tests/*.hurl`
   Hurl also supports `--variables-file` for per-environment values and `--parallel` for speed.

**Runner-up: Bruno CLI**
Bruno is a free, open-source GUI client whose collections are plain-text files in a folder you can commit. The CLI (`npm install -g @usebruno/cli`, which requires Node) runs them with `bru run`, and it supports `--env`, `--bail`, and JUnit/HTML reports. Choose it if your team wants a GUI and JavaScript assertions. Its CLI flags have changed across versions, so check the current reference first. Also, secret variables aren't exposed to the CLI, so you pass them explicitly.

- [Bruno CLI quick start](https://docs.usebruno.com/bru-cli/quick-start)
- [Bruno CLI blog](https://blog.usebruno.com/bruno-cli)
